In [[Euclidean geometry]], an '''equiangular polygon''' is a [[polygon]] whose vertex angles are equal. If the lengths of the sides are also equal (that is, if it is also [[equilateral polygon|equilateral]]) then it is a [[regular polygon]]. [[Isogonal polygon]]s are equiangular polygons which alternate two edge lengths.

For clarity, a '''planar equiangular polygon''' can be called ''direct'' or ''indirect''. A '''direct equiangular polygon''' has all angles turning in the same direction in a plane and can include multiple [[turn (angle)|turns]]. '''Convex equiangular polygons''' are always direct. An '''indirect equiangular polygon''' can include angles turning right or left in any combination. A '''[[skew polygon|skew]] equiangular polygon''' may be [[isogonal figure|isogonal]], but can't be considered direct since it is nonplanar.

A [[spirolateral]] ''n''<sub>&theta;</sub> is a special case of an ''equiangular polygon'' with a set of ''n'' integer edge lengths repeating sequence until returning to the start, with vertex internal angles &theta;.

== Construction==
An ''equiangular polygon'' can be constructed from a [[regular polygon]] or [[regular star polygon]] where edges are extended as infinite [[Line (geometry)|line]]s. Each edges can be independently moved perpendicular to the line's direction. Vertices represent the intersection point between pairs of neighboring line. Each moved line adjusts its edge-length and the lengths of its two neighboring edges.<ref>Marius Munteanu, Laura Munteanu, [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/271296486_Rational_Equiangular_Polygons Rational Equiangular Polygons] Applied Mathematics, Vol.4 No.10, October 2013</ref> If edges are reduced to zero length, the polygon becomes degenerate, or if reduced to ''negative'' lengths, this will reverse the internal and external angles.

For an even-sided direct equiangular polygon, with internal angles &theta;°, moving alternate edges can invert all vertices into [[supplementary angle]]s, 180-&theta;°. Odd-sided direct equiangular polygons can only be partially inverted, leaving a mixture of supplementary angles.

Every equiangular polygon can be adjusted in proportions by this construction and still preserve equiangular status.

{| class=wikitable width=320
|[[File:Equiangular hexagon-example.png|160px]]<BR>This convex ''direct equiangular hexagon'', {{angbr|6}}, is bounded by 6 [[Line (geometry)|lines]] with 60° angle between. Each line can be moved perpendicular to its direction.
|[[File:Indirect equiangular polygon.png|160px]]<BR>This concave ''indirect equiangular hexagon'', {{angbr|6-2}}, is also bounded by 6 lines with 90° angle between, each line moved independently, moving vertices as new intersections.
|}

==Equiangular polygon theorem==
For a ''convex equiangular'' ''p''-gon, each [[internal angle]] is 180(1&minus;2/''p'')°; this is the ''equiangular polygon theorem''.

For a direct equiangular ''p''/''q'' [[star polygon]], [[density (geometry)|density]] ''q'', each internal angle is 180(1&minus;2''q''/''p'')°, with {{math|1 < 2''q'' < ''p''}}. For {{math|1=''w'' = gcd(''p'',''q'') > 1}}, this represents a ''w''-wound {{sfrac|''p''/''w''|''q''/''w''}} star polygon, which is degenerate for the regular case.

A concave ''indirect equiangular'' {{math|(''p''<sub>''r''</sub>+''p''<sub>''l''</sub>)}}-gon, with {{math|''p''<sub>''r''</sub>}} right turn vertices and {{math|''p''<sub>''l''</sub>}} left turn vertices, will have internal angles of {{math|180(1&minus;2/{{abs|''p''<sub>''r''</sub>&minus;''p''<sub>''l''</sub>}}))°}}, regardless of their sequence. An ''indirect star equiangular'' {{math|(''p''<sub>''r''</sub>+''p''<sub>''l''</sub>)}}-gon, with {{math|''p''<sub>''r''</sub>}} right turn vertices and {{math|''p''<sub>''l''</sub>}} left turn vertices and ''q'' total [[turn (angle)|turns]], will have internal angles of {{math|180(1&minus;2''q''/{{abs|''p''<sub>''r''</sub>&minus;''p''<sub>''l''</sub>}}))°}}, regardless of their sequence. An equiangular polygon with the same number of right and left turns has zero total turns, and has no constraints on its angles.

== Notation ==
Every direct equiangular ''p''-gon can be given a notation {{angbr|''p''}} or {{angbr|''p''/''q''}}, like [[regular polygon]]s {''p''} and [[regular star polygon]]s {''p''/''q''}, containing ''p'' vertices, and stars having [[Density (polytope)#Polygons|density]] ''q''.

Convex equiangular ''p''-gons {{angbr|''p''}} have internal angles 180(1&minus;2/''p'')°, while direct star equiangular polygons, {{angbr|''p''/''q''}}, have internal angles 180(1&minus;2''q''/''p'')°.

A concave indirect equiangular ''p''-gon can be given the notation {{angbr|''p''&minus;2''c''}}, with ''c'' counter-turn vertices. For example, {{angbr|6&minus;2}} is a hexagon with 90° internal angles of the difference, {{angbr|4}}, 1 counter-turned vertex. A multiturn indirect equilateral ''p''-gon can be given the notation {{angbr|<sup>''p''&minus;2''c''</sup>/<sub>''q''</sub>}}  with ''c'' counter turn vertices, and ''q'' total [[turn (angle)|turns]]. An equiangular polygon <''p''&minus;''p''> is a ''p''-gon with undefined internal angles {{mvar|&theta;}}, but can be expressed explicitly as {{angbr|''p''&minus;''p''}}<sub>''&theta;''</sub>.

==Other properties==
[[Viviani's theorem]] holds for equiangular polygons:<ref name="ref1">{{cite journal |title=Viviani's Theorem and Its Extension |first=Elias |last=Abboud |journal=The College Mathematics Journal |volume=41 |issue=3 |year=2010 |pages=203-211 |doi=10.4169/074683410x488683 }}</ref>
:''The sum of distances from an interior point to the sides of an equiangular polygon does not depend on the location of the point, and is that polygon's invariant.''

A [[cyclic polygon]] is equiangular if and only if the alternate sides are equal (that is, sides 1, 3, 5, ... are equal and sides 2, 4, ... are equal). Thus if ''n'' is odd, a cyclic polygon is equiangular if and only if it is regular.<ref>De Villiers, Michael, "Equiangular cyclic and equilateral circumscribed polygons", [[Mathematical Gazette]] 95, March 2011, 102-107.</ref>

For prime ''p'', every integer-sided equiangular ''p''-gon is regular. Moreover, every integer-sided equiangular ''p''<sup>''k''</sup>-gon has ''p''-fold [[rotational symmetry]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=McLean |first=K. Robin |title=A powerful algebraic tool for equiangular polygons |journal=Mathematical Gazette |issue=88 |year=2004 |pages=513-514 |doi=10.1017/S002555720017617X}}</ref>

An ordered set of side lengths <math>(a_1, \dots , a_n)</math> gives rise to an equiangular ''n''-gon if and only if either of two equivalent conditions holds for the polynomial <math>a_1+a_2x+\cdots + a_{n-1}x^{n-2}+a_nx^{n-1}:</math> it equals zero at the complex value <math>e^{2\pi i/n};</math> it is divisible by <math>x^2-2x \cos (2\pi /n)+1.</math><ref>{{cite journal |first1=M. |last1=Bras-Amorós |first2=M. |last2=Pujol |title=Side Lengths of Equiangular Polygons (as seen by a coding theorist) |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=122 |issue=5 |pages=476–478 |year=2015 |doi=10.4169/amer.math.monthly.122.5.476 }}</ref>
{{clear|left}}

== Direct equiangular polygons by sides ==
Direct equiangular polygons can be regular, isogonal, or lower symmetries. Examples for &lt;''p''/''q''&gt; are grouped into sections by ''p'' and subgrouped by density ''q''.

=== Equiangular triangles===
'''Equiangular triangles''' must be convex and have 60° internal angles. It is an [[equilateral triangle]] and a [[regular triangle]], {{angbr|3}}={3}. The only degree of freedom is edge-length.
<gallery>
Regular polygon 3 annotated.svg|Regular, {3}, r<sub>6</sub>
</gallery>

=== Equiangular quadrilaterals ===
[[File:Rectangle-2x3.svg|thumb|A rectangle dissected into a 2×3 array of squares<ref name="ball"/>]]
Direct '''equiangular quadrilaterals''' have 90° internal angles. The only equiangular quadrilaterals are [[rectangle]]s, {{angbr|4}}, and [[square]]s, {4}.

An equiangular quadrilateral with integer side lengths may be tiled by [[unit square]]s.<ref name="ball">{{citation|first=Derek|last=Ball|title=Equiangular polygons|journal=The Mathematical Gazette|volume=86|issue=507|year=2002|pages=396–407|doi=10.2307/3621131|jstor=3621131|s2cid=233358516}}.</ref>

</gallery>
